scope: Glossary entries on Kant and Hegel along the route from Spinoza to Deleuze and Land: phenomenon and noumenon, transcendental, synthetic a priori, dialectic, Aufhebung, idealism

old.text: Phenomena under space, time and categories; the noumenon or thing in itself, which we cannot know.
Kant distinguishes a negative sense of noumenon from a positive sense (an object of an intellectual intuition we lack).
old.note: Not in the sources consulted; cut.

old.text: Things in themselves cannot be known yet must be thinkable; practical reason gives grounds for belief in freedom, God and immortality.
old.note: Thinkable-but-unknowable kept from Stang; the practical-reason clause has no source consulted, cut.

old.text: Fichte and Hegel judged an unknowable thing in itself incoherent, which set German idealism on its course.
old.note: Stang reports the affection objection (Jacobi, Fichte); Redding's reading of Hegel quoted; the causal claim about German idealism cut.

old.text: Land's collected essays take their title, Fanged Noumena, from the term.

new_d.text: Kant: phenomena are things as they appear to us, under the forms of space and time and the categories. The noumenon, or thing in itself, is reality as it is independent of us, which we cannot know.

new_text.text: Nicholas Stang sums up the doctrine: space and time are “the forms of our sensible intuition of objects”, and “We cannot cognize things in themselves”, though we can think about them using the categories.
Kant calls the thing in itself “something actual for itself but uncognized by us”, and interpreters divide between a two-objects and a two-aspects reading of the distinction.

Jacobi, and Fichte after him, objected that Kant's account of affection is inconsistent: the objects that affect our senses can be neither things in themselves, since that would apply the categories to them, nor appearances, which depend on the very experiences they would cause; Jacobi wrote that “without the presupposition of the [thing in itself] I cannot enter the [critical] system”.
Paul Redding reports that post-Kantian interpreters see Hegel as furthering Kant's critique “into the very coherence of a conception of an in-itself reality”.
Nick Land's collected writings of 1987–2007 are titled Fanged Noumena.

noumenon.s: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, Bxix–xx, A235–60/B294–315

old.text: Concerning the conditions that make experience possible; a transcendental argument shows what must hold for experience.
Kant calls transcendental the cognition occupied with our way of knowing objects insofar as possible a priori.
old.note: B25 not found in the sources consulted; cut, locator kept.

old.text: The transcendental deduction argues that the categories must apply to anything we can experience.
Fichte built his system on the transcendental I; Husserl's transcendental phenomenology.
old.note: No source consulted; cut. Deleuze's transcendental empiricism added from the checked Deleuze entry.

old.text: Keep apart from “transcendent”, passing the limits of possible experience.

new_d.text: In Kant, concerning the a priori conditions of the possibility of experience. A transcendental argument begins from a compelling premise about thought, experience or knowledge and reasons to “a substantive and unobvious presupposition and necessary condition” of it.

new_text.text: Kant holds that the categories “must be recognized as a priori conditions of the possibility of experiences”.
His transcendental deduction aims to show, against the classical empiricists, that some a priori concepts hold of the objects we experience.
The Transcendental Dialectic, which treats transcendent claims beyond experience, sets out “to expose the illusion in transcendent judgments”.
Deleuze faults Kant for modelling the transcendental on the empirical, and called his own position “transcendental empiricism”.

transcendental.s: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, B25, A84–130/B116–69, A297/B354

old.text: Judgments that add content and are known independently of experience: arithmetic, geometry, every event has a cause.
“How are synthetic judgments a priori possible?” organizes the Critique.
old.note: Rey: its possibility became a major concern of Kant's work; the question as worded is not in the sources consulted.

old.text: Kant's answer: space and time forms of intuition, categories forms of understanding.
Critics argued that non-Euclidean geometry and relativity undercut his examples; the logical empiricists denied any synthetic a priori knowledge.
old.note: Restated as the source has it.

new_d.text: Kant's claim that some judgments add content to their concepts and are still known independently of experience.

new_text.text: Georges Rey writes that the possibility of the synthetic a priori “became a major concern” of Kant's work, and that Kant argued that “even so elementary an example in arithmetic as 7+5=12 is synthetic”; his concern extended to geometry as well.
Kant treats the law that every event has a cause as one that the sensible world conforms to and that can be known a priori.

His answer is that sensibility contributes space and time as a priori forms of intuition and the understanding contributes the categories, so that “we can cognize of things a priori only what we ourselves have put into them”.

In the nineteenth century Gauss, Riemann and Lobachevsky developed non-Euclidean geometries as conceptual possibilities, and in 1916 Einstein argued that physics seemed to favour one of them over Euclid's.
The logical positivists hoped logical analysis would show that the rest of our knowledge, beyond mathematics, rests on logic and experience combined.

synthetic-a-priori.s: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, Bxviii, B14–19; Prolegomena (1783), §5

old.text: Hegel's dialectic as movement through contradiction into a richer form; “thesis, antithesis, synthesis” from Fichte, never Hegel's for his own philosophy.
Plato's dialectic rises toward the Forms; Kant's transcendental dialectic exposes reason's illusions.
old.note: Restated as Maybee describes Plato and Kant.

old.text: Self-movement of concepts through determinate negation.
Marx and Engels gave it a materialist form; Adorno's negative dialectics refuses Hegel's final reconciliation.
old.note: Marx and Engels not in the sources consulted, cut; Adorno in Zuidervaart's words.

new_d.text: In Hegel, the movement by which a concept or form produces its own contradictions and passes into a richer one. The formula “thesis—antithesis—synthesis” is Fichte's; Hegel never adopted it to describe his own philosophy.

new_text.text: Plato's dialectic is a back-and-forth dialogue, mainly between Socrates and his interlocutors, that refines views over time.
Kant held that reason generates contradictions, the antinomies, and Hegel took up his idea of a self-driving reason while arguing that the contradictions are objective.

Julie Maybee describes the outcome of each stage of Hegel's dialectic as “a determinate nothingness, one which has a content”, from which, in Hegel's words, “a new form has thereby immediately arisen”.
Adorno calls dialectics “the consistent consciousness of nonidentity”, and Lambert Zuidervaart explains why he rejects the affirmative character of Hegel's dialectic.

dialectic.s: Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807), Preface; Science of Logic (1812–16); Adorno, Negative Dialectics (1966)

old.text: Overcoming that cancels, preserves and lifts up.
old.note: Cancel and preserve confirmed; 'lifts up' not in the sources consulted.

old.text: Hegel delights that aufheben means both to cancel and to preserve; what is sublated survives as a moment.
old.note: The double meaning kept; Hegel's delight not in the sources consulted.

old.text: Translations: sublation, supersession, overcoming.
Being, nothing and becoming at the opening of the Logic; each later category arises the same way.
old.note: The opening kept; the general claim cut.

new_d.text: Hegel's term for an overcoming that at once cancels and preserves what it overcomes.

new_text.text: The German verb aufheben means both to cancel or negate and to preserve, and English writers render it as “sublate”.
Paul Redding glosses what is sublated as “aufgehoben, with a sense of being negated but still preserved”.

The Science of Logic opens with an example: pure being, with no determination, is no different from nothing, and passes into it; becoming unites the two as “the immediate vanishing of the one in the other”, and is the Logic's first concrete concept.

aufhebung.s: Hegel, Science of Logic, Book One, ch. 1, Remark on the expression “sublation”

old.text: Reality fundamentally mental, or the known world mind-dependent; Berkeley, Kant and Hegel very different.
Berkeley: esse est percipi; things as collections of ideas sustained by God's perception.
Kant: space, time and categories forms of our cognition; we know things only as they appear.
Hegel's absolute idealism: reality as the self-development of spirit or reason, grasped as a whole.
old.note: Redding presents absolute idealism as the traditional reading; given as such.

old.text: Marx turned Hegel's dialectic toward material conditions.

new_d.text: The view that “something mental (the mind, spirit, reason, will) is the ultimate foundation of all reality, or even exhaustive of reality”; an epistemological form holds that all knowledge is in some sense self-knowledge.

new_text.text: Horstmann reconstructs Berkeley's central claim as “the existence of an idea consists in being perceived”, which leads him to treat things as ideal entities in God's mind.
Kant's transcendental idealism holds that space and time belong only to our representations of things, to things as they appear to us; they are no real properties of things in themselves.

Paul Redding describes the traditional metaphysical reading of Hegel as an absolute idealism, in which both subjective life and the cultural practices it depends on belong to God's development as Absolute Spirit.

idealism.s: Berkeley, A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710), §3; Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (1781/1787); Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807)
